Later, when she has gone upstairs to dress and he is washing the cups, he stands at the sink with his hands in hot water and thinks: she will or she won't, and either way he will be here, and either way the house has just acquired a second door, and the door has always been there, and he had not known until this morning that he had been the one to keep it closed.
pieces.notes: Present tense, kitchen-set negotiation between a long-married couple; the erotic is entirely in trust, articulation, and what is conceded — no physical scene at all.

pieces.title: Office Hours, Late
pieces.excerpt: She had not been his student in eleven years. The corridor outside the office still smelled the same — paper, radiator dust, the faint clove of someone's tea — and that was the first thing that undid her, before he had even opened the door.
pieces.body:
She had not been his student in eleven years. The corridor outside the office still smelled the same — paper, radiator dust, the faint clove of someone's tea — and that was the first thing that undid her, before he had even opened the door.

She had been twenty when she sat in his seminar on the long nineteenth-century novel, and he had been forty-one, and the gap had been an ocean. She had written him an email at the end of that term thanking him for a single sentence he had said about Middlemarch, and he had written back two paragraphs that she had printed and kept in a folder for years and then, eventually, lost in a move. She had not spoken to him in person since the day of her viva, where he had sat at the back of the room and said nothing and shaken her hand afterwards and called her by her surname for the first time, as though to release her into the world as a peer.

Now she was thirty-one. She had a book out, a small one, with a press he respected. She had written to him three months ago to ask if she could buy him a drink when she was in the city, and he had written back to suggest his office at six, after his last meeting, and a walk to a bar he liked, and she had said yes.

The door opened. He was greyer. The grey suited him; she had expected it to and was annoyed at having been right. He was thinner too, in a way that suggested either illness or a recent and successful negotiation with himself, and she did not yet know which.

"Come in," he said. "I'm just packing up."

The office was the same office. The desk, the lamp, the shelves with the same broken order. A new framed photograph she did not look at. He moved papers and she stood, because she had not been invited to sit, and because sitting in that chair, the chair she had sat in at twenty, would have been a thing she could not yet bring herself to do.

"It's good to see you," he said, without looking at her. "I read the book."

"Oh."

"It's very good."

"You're being kind."

"I'm not, actually. I don't, anymore. There isn't time."

She smiled at the floor. He looked up at the smile, and she saw him register it, and saw him decide to register it openly. The decision was new. The man she had known at twenty would not have let her see him notice anything.

They walked to the bar. The walk was long enough for the city to do its evening work on them. The bar was the kind of place he would choose — old wood, a stained ceiling, a long mirror behind the bottles in which she could see, when she looked up, the two of them sitting side by side at the counter, looking like what they were not.

He ordered for both of them without asking. She let him, because she was curious what he remembered, and he remembered. The drink was the one she had not had in years, the one she had picked up from him in the first place, at a department gathering she had no business attending. She had been twenty-one then, in a borrowed dress. He had been very correct. He had been very correct for the entire eight terms she had known him.

"How long are you in town," he said.

"Two more days."

"Where are you staying."

She told him. He nodded. He did not say anything else for a minute. She watched, in the long mirror, his fingers on the stem of his glass — the same fingers that had marked up her essays once, a careful, almost calligraphic hand in soft pencil. She remembered every comment. She had read each of them in her room with the door closed and her face hot, not because the comments were intimate — they had been the opposite of intimate, they had been clean — but because the cleanness itself, the attention, had been more than anyone had ever paid her.

"You're allowed to ask me anything now," he said.

"Now meaning."

"Now meaning you don't owe me anything and I don't owe you anything, and you're not twenty."

She took a sip of her drink. "Were you ever — " She did not finish.

"Yes," he said. "Of course. I was very careful not to be, but yes."

The bar around them did not stop. Two men were arguing about a film at the far end of the counter. The bartender was cutting a lime. Outside, a tram passed and rang its bell. She set her glass down because her hand had gone, suddenly, a little unreliable.

"You never — "

"No. And I wouldn't have. I want to be very clear about that, because I think it matters that you know."

"I know."

"I know you know. I wanted to say it anyway."

She nodded. She did not trust her voice yet. She thought about all the small evidences she had collected, over the years, of his having seen her — the slight pause once when she had spoken in seminar, the way he had read her name from the list on the first day with a faint, particular attention, the email after the viva that had said only well done and her surname and his initial. She had built, out of those things, a small private cathedral, and had eventually stopped going inside it, and now he had handed her the key back and confirmed that the building was real.

"What changed," she said.

"Time. You're thirty-one. I'm fifty-two. The arithmetic is the same and the meaning of the arithmetic is different."

"That's a sentence you've thought about."

"For some years, yes."

She laughed, and the laugh undid something in her chest. He looked at her then properly, full on, and she looked back, and for a long moment neither of them did anything with the look. It sat between them on the wooden counter like a third drink.

"Walk me back," she said, eventually.

He paid. They walked. The city had got colder. He did not offer her his coat, which she appreciated, because the gesture would have been the wrong one and he had always known the right gesture, even at the cost of seeming to feel less than he felt. At the door of her hotel he stopped a little short of the awning, in a patch of pavement that was not lit.

"I'm not going to come up," he said.

"I know."

"I would like to."

"I know."

"I want you to know that I would like to. I think you should have that, after this long."

She looked at him and the years between them stood up around them, in the cold, like a small crowd that had been waiting all evening to be acknowledged. She put her hand, briefly, on the front of his coat — flat, the way one rests a hand on a door one is about to leave closed — and felt his breath go in, and out. He did not lift his hand to cover hers. He let her have the gesture. That was what she remembered, later, more than anything: that he had let her have the gesture, undefended, and had not made her share it.

"Goodnight," she said.

"Goodnight, Anna."

It was the first time he had ever said her first name. She walked into the hotel and did not look back until she was inside the lift, and by then the doors were closing, and the street where he had stood was already a slot of dark glass narrowing to nothing, and she stood very still in the small bright box and rode it up, and her hand, on the rail, was shaking, and the eleven years she had carried him for were settling at last, in her, into something she could finally set down.
pieces.notes: Past tense, professor and former student eleven years on; the erotic charge is the explicit acknowledgement of what was never acted on, and the conscious choice to still not act.

pieces.title: Saturday at the Linden
pieces.excerpt: The bar is below street level and the stairs down to it are painted black, and every Saturday at eleven the music starts to do that thing it does — not louder, exactly, but lower, settling into the room like a second floor laid over the first.
pieces.body:
The bar is below street level and the stairs down to it are painted black, and every Saturday at eleven the music starts to do that thing it does — not louder, exactly, but lower, settling into the room like a second floor laid over the first. June comes down the stairs and the bouncer, who knows her, doesn't ask for ID, just lifts her wrist gently and presses the stamp onto the soft inside above the pulse. The stamp is a small linden leaf. The bar is called the Linden. The leaves have been the same for years.

Inside, the light is the colour of weak whisky. There are red bulbs over the bar and amber ones over the booths and a single greenish strip behind the DJ that makes the bottles look like specimens. June takes the room in the way she always does: the regulars at the far booth, the new ones near the door pretending not to look around, the bartender Hugo who lifts two fingers in greeting without breaking conversation. She lifts two fingers back. She is not lonely. She is not looking for anyone in particular. She is here because Saturday is the night her week makes sense.

She orders a beer and stands at the corner of the bar where she can watch both the dance floor and the door. The dance floor is small — maybe twelve people, maybe fifteen — and the music tonight is slow and old, a track she remembers from a different bar in a different city, a song that goes around once and then twice and then doesn't quite end. A tall woman in a mesh shirt is dancing with someone shorter and broader, their foreheads close, hands at each other's hips, not moving much. Near them a person in a soft sleeveless tank is swaying alone with their eyes closed, an unbothered private smile on their face, and June feels a quick warm gladness at the sight of them, the way one is glad of a window left lit in a building one walks past at night.

"You came," someone says at her shoulder.

It is Rey, who June has known for two years and slept with once and is now glad to count as a friend, which is rarer and harder than the other thing. Rey kisses her on the cheek — dry, quick, the way people who have decided not to be lovers kiss — and orders something complicated that Hugo makes without comment.

"You always say you're not coming and you always come," Rey says.

"I always mean it when I say it."

"I know. That's what makes it nice."

They stand together at the corner of the bar and watch the room. Rey points out, with small movements of their chin, the people June should know about: someone new from out of town, someone back after a long absence, someone whose ex just walked in and who is being very, very careful not to look. June takes it all in. She loves this — the cartography of the room, the small civic awareness that everyone here keeps of everyone else. It is one of the things she loves most about this kind of place. People notice. People look out. The brushing past is not accidental.

The song changes. The new one is slower still, a bassline that feels like a hand on the back of the neck. The dance floor shifts. A few people leave it, a few more step on. June feels, without quite deciding to, her own weight transfer onto the balls of her feet.

"Go," Rey says, without looking at her.

"I haven't said anything."

"You're vibrating. Go."

She goes. She sets her beer on the shelf above the radiator where the regulars always set their drinks, and she steps down onto the dance floor, and the music takes her in the way it always does, which is to say not all at once. She closes her eyes for the first thirty seconds. She lets her shoulders go. She lets her hips find the count. When she opens her eyes again, the room has rearranged itself around her without her noticing, the way it always does — the small constellation of bodies has accepted a new star.

There is someone next to her she has not seen before. Tall, soft-jawed, in a white t-shirt that has been washed enough times to lie close to the skin. They are dancing with their eyes mostly down, the small private dance of someone who is not yet sure whether they belong here and is deciding, song by song, that they do. June recognises the feeling. She had it for a long time herself. She gives them a sliver of a smile when they look up, the kind of smile that says I see you, that's all, you don't have to do anything about it. They smile back, surprised, grateful, and look down again.

The song shifts into the next song without seam. Hugo at the bar leans across to change a bottle. The mesh-shirt woman has her hand flat against the small of her partner's back now, fingers spread, and they are barely moving, and the not-moving is the whole of the conversation. June feels the bass in her sternum. She feels the warm press of the room — bodies close but not crowding, the polite physics of a good night, where everyone has agreed, without ever discussing it, on how much space a stranger may take.

The person in the white t-shirt has drifted half a step closer. Not enough to be a question. Enough to be an offer.

June does not close the distance. She does not move away either. She keeps dancing. After a while their elbow grazes hers — the lightest contact, the kind one might have on a crowded train and not register — and she does not pull her arm away, and they do not pull theirs, and the brush stays, a continuous low note under the music. She becomes aware of their breathing, somewhere just to her right, slightly faster than the song. She becomes aware of her own.

She turns her head, finally, and looks at them. Their eyes come up to meet hers, and there is in their face exactly what she had hoped to find — not hunger, not yet, but the openness that has to come before hunger if any of it is going to be any good. June leans in, not far, just enough that her mouth is near their ear.

"What's your name," she says.

They tell her. She tells them hers. The exchange is not loud enough to be heard by anyone else, and the smallness of it, in the middle of the bass, is itself a kind of intimacy. The person in the white t-shirt's smile, when she draws back, is shy and entirely undefended, and June thinks: oh, you. Oh, careful. Be careful with this one.

She does not invite them anywhere. She does not have to. They dance the rest of the song side by side, hands almost touching, the back of her wrist passing the back of theirs once, twice, a private metronome under the public music. When the song ends she rests her hand on their forearm, briefly, the way one might on the arm of a friend one is leaving for a moment, and walks off the floor toward the bar to get them both a drink.

At the bar Hugo already has two glasses out. He has been watching, the way Hugo watches, with the half-smile of someone who has seen this evening go a thousand ways and is glad to see it going this one. Rey lifts a brow from the corner. June lifts a shoulder back. The whole exchange takes a second. The room holds her like the room has always held her — close, knowing, kind — and she carries the two drinks back across the floor, and the bass goes on under the soles of her boots, and the person in the white t-shirt turns to watch her come, and the night, which is not yet half over, has already given her everything she came down those black stairs to find.
pieces.notes: Present tense, queer bar scene rendered through music, light, and the etiquette of the room; the eroticism is communal and tender, almost no body description, all atmosphere and consent-shaped attention.

pieces.title: Letter I Will Not Send
pieces.excerpt: I wrote your name on the inside of my wrist last Tuesday in pen, just to see if I could still spell it without flinching. I could. That, I think, was the worst part.
pieces.body:
I wrote your name on the inside of my wrist last Tuesday in pen, just to see if I could still spell it without flinching. I could. That, I think, was the worst part. Three syllables, the loop of the second letter the way you always made it, the small crooked finish — and then nothing. No tremor, no heat, no pulse in the throat. The body, it turned out, had filed you away with the rest of the dead languages.

I am writing this from the kitchen of the apartment you have never seen. There is a window above the sink, and beyond it the brick wall of another building so close you could spit and hit it, and between the two walls a kind of soft grey weather that I have come to call mine. I bought the chairs alone. I bought the bowls alone. I learned, alone, that I prefer my coffee bitter, which surprised me, because for two years I drank it the way you took yours and called that taste love.

What I want to tell you is small. It is not a confession in the operatic sense. I am not going to write that I dream of you, because I don't, or not often, and when I do you appear at the edge of the dream like a coat someone left on a chair. What I want to tell you is that on Thursday I was buying lemons and the man at the register had your hands. Just that. The same blunt thumbs, the same way of folding a paper bag down twice and creasing it, as if a paper bag were a letter that needed sealing. I stood there with my lemons and I felt the floor go thin under me, the way it used to when you would come up behind me in the hallway and not touch me — just stand there, just breathe — and I would feel the entire shape of you against the entire shape of me without a single point of contact.

You used to do that on purpose. I know you did. You used to count, I think, how long I could stand it before I turned around.

I am not going to write about the bed. I promised myself when I sat down that I would not write about the bed, and I won't, not directly. But I will say this: there was a way you had of stopping. Of bringing a thing almost to its given conclusion and then, very deliberately, withdrawing the hand or the mouth or the weight of you, and letting me feel the absence as if it were a second body. You called it patience. I called it nothing because I had no word for it then. I have a word for it now. I am not going to write it down.

The woman I am seeing is kind. I want to be clear about that, in case this letter ever finds you, in case some impossible weather carries it across the years and the two cities and the marriage you are presumably still inside of. She is kind. She laughs with her whole chest. She does not stop. She arrives and arrives and arrives, and afterward she falls asleep with her hand open on my hip, palm up, like a small dish waiting for rain. I am learning, slowly, what it is to be loved without being studied. It is a quieter country. There are fewer mirrors in it.

But I wanted you to know — and this is the part I have been circling, the part the whole letter exists to deliver and then bury — that I understood, finally, what you were doing. Not at the time. At the time I thought it was cruelty dressed as restraint, and I forgave it because I was twenty-six and I mistook every withholding for depth. I thought later it was cowardice. For a long stretch in my early thirties I was certain it was cowardice, and I hated you with the clean specific hatred one reserves for people who taught one to want something they had no intention of giving. But it wasn't cowardice. I see that now. You were teaching me how to live inside a wanting that would not be answered. You were teaching me, in the only language you had, that the body's deepest pleasure is sometimes the pleasure of not being delivered. You did not know you were teaching me. You thought you were just being careful. The most precise educations are always accidental.

I use it now, what you taught me. I use it badly and I use it well. I use it when I write. I use it when I am with her, and I am not proud of this, I am not proud of carrying you into a bed that was supposed to be free of you — but there it is. The pause before the kiss. The hand that hovers. The sentence I leave unfinished because I have learned that the unfinished sentence is the one the listener finishes inside their own mouth, and that is the sentence they will remember.

It is raining now, properly, against the brick. I have made the coffee. The cup is the small blue one I bought at the market the week I moved in, the week I cried in the produce aisle over a bag of apples for reasons I could not at the time name. I can name them now. I was crying because no one was watching me cry. I had spent two years being watched, even when you were not in the room, especially when you were not in the room — you had installed a small attentive version of yourself behind my eyes, and it took me a year of solitude to evict him, and another year to forgive the apartment for being empty of him.

I am not asking you anything. I want to be very clear about that, too. There is no question at the end of this letter. There is no address on the envelope. There will be no envelope. I will fold this in half when I am done and I will put it in the drawer with the others, and one day, when I am old or brave or finally bored of you, I will burn the drawer.

What I wanted, I think, was simply to say it out loud in a room you could not enter. To put a small intact sentence on a page and have it be true: I loved you badly and you loved me carefully, and between those two failures we made something I have not been able to match since, and may not want to. The thing we made was not a relationship. It was a kind of weather. It is still my weather. I walk around inside it. I am writing to you from the middle of it now.

It is enough. It has to be enough.

I am going to put the pen down. I am going to wash the cup. She will be here at seven and I will not have showered and she will laugh at me and pull me toward the bedroom by two fingers hooked into the waistband of whatever I am wearing, and I will go, and I will be glad to go, and somewhere under the gladness, very quiet, almost inaudible, the small attentive version of you that I could not entirely evict will turn his head to listen.

Goodnight. I hope you are well. I hope you are not.
pieces.notes: Confessional unsent letter, present-day apartment, second-person address; restraint and the eroticism of withholding as the central image; queer narrator with current partner.

pieces.title: The Room with the Wrong Key
pieces.excerpt: The hotel had given us the wrong key, and we did not tell the desk. For one entire night we lived inside a room that wasn't ours, in a city neither of us was supposed to be in, and used the wrong towels with a thoroughness that felt, by morning, like a vow.
pieces.body:
The hotel had given us the wrong key, and we did not tell the desk. For one entire night we lived inside a room that wasn't ours, in a city neither of us was supposed to be in, and used the wrong towels with a thoroughness that felt, by morning, like a vow.

I remember the corridor first. The carpet was a deep, almost wet red, the kind of red old buildings still allow themselves, and the wall sconces had small parchment shades the color of weak tea. He walked half a pace ahead of me with the key card held the way a child holds a found feather, as if any sudden gesture might cost him the thing. I was carrying nothing. I had come from a dinner I had pretended to enjoy, and my coat smelled of someone else's cigarettes, and my mouth, when I ran my tongue along the back of my teeth, still tasted of the wine they had poured too generously and I had drunk too slowly, watching the door.

The lock made the small green sound. He pushed the door open with his shoulder and let me go in first, and I remember stopping in the doorway because the room was wrong. It was too big. There were two armchairs by a window I had not been promised, and a writing desk under a lamp already lit, and a bed turned down on both sides with a small dark chocolate on each pillow, which is the universal hotel signal that a room is occupied. Someone else had paid for this room. Someone else's suitcase, I realized after a slow second, was open on the luggage rack, neat as a sentence — folded shirts, a paperback face down, a leather case for cufflinks.

He came in behind me and closed the door very quietly and we stood there, the two of us, in the foyer of a stranger's evening, and he said, without looking at me, we should go back down. And I said, without looking at him, in a moment. And we did not go back down.

I cannot fully explain what happened in me then. I was thirty-one. I was, in the rest of my life, a person who returned the extra change. But there was something about the wrongness of the room that undid a small careful seam in me. It made the night feel borrowed in a way that absolved it. We were not really here. The bed was not really ours. Whatever we did in this room would belong to the man whose shirts were folded on the rack, and he would carry it home in his suitcase without ever knowing, and that struck me, standing there in my coat that smelled of strangers, as the closest thing to permission I had been given in months.

He took the coat off me. I want to be precise about this, because I have thought about it for years and the precision matters. He did not pull it off. He stood behind me and slid his hands under the lapels at the collar and lifted, and the coat went down my arms with the slow obedience of a thing being undressed by someone who had undressed it many times before, although he had never undressed anything of mine. He hung it in the closet. He hung it on a wooden hanger that did not belong to me, in a room that did not belong to me, and the small domestic competence of that gesture — the hanger, the closet, the soft click of the closet door — almost finished me before anything had begun.

We did not turn off the desk lamp. I want to say that too. The whole night was lit by that one lamp, the color of a held breath, and the rest of the room stayed in a softness that was not quite dark, so that I could see the shape of him moving but not the detail, and he could see the shape of me. There is a particular mercy in that kind of light. It lets you be braver than you are.

He sat on the edge of the bed and looked at me for a long time without touching me. This was not, I understood even then, a hesitation. He was deciding something, or letting me decide it, and the deciding was the first act of what we did. I crossed the room slowly because I wanted him to watch me cross it. I stopped in front of him close enough that my knees touched his knees, and he put one hand, just one, flat against the small of my back, low, where the spine begins to become something else, and held it there. He did not pull. He simply rested his hand against me with a steadiness that I felt all the way up into my throat. We stayed like that. I do not know for how long. Long enough that the cold of the room left me. Long enough that I understood the rest of the night was going to be told in this register — in pauses, in held positions, in the slow accumulation of a single touch into a sentence.

What I did, what we did — I will not write it down. Not because I am ashamed. I am not ashamed. I will not write it down because it belongs to that room, and to the lamp, and to the soft red corridor outside, and to the man whose paperback lay face down on the desk and whose night we were quietly hollowing out a space inside of. It belongs, also, to a version of me I am no longer in possession of, a version who could walk into a stranger's room and decide, in the dim of a borrowed lamp, that the wrongness of it was the most honest thing she had encountered in a year.

What I will tell you is this: at some point, hours in, he laughed. Quietly, into the place where my neck becomes my shoulder, a small private laugh that was not at me and not at himself but at the whole improbable arrangement, the fact of us, the chocolates on the pillows we had pushed aside, the fact that somewhere in the building the actual occupant of this room was perhaps standing at a hotel desk explaining in a tired voice that his key would not work. And I laughed too, into his hair, and the laugh did something to the rhythm of what we were doing that I have been chasing in every bed since and have not, not quite, found again.

We slept a little. Not much. Toward dawn I got up and stood by the window in one of the hotel's robes — also not mine, also borrowed — and watched the city begin the long pale business of being itself again. The river was the color of pewter. A single barge moved on it with the patience of an old animal. He came up behind me and did not touch me. He stood close enough that I could feel the heat of him along the entire back of me, and far enough that there was, between us, a thin clear margin of cold air, and we breathed together in that margin for what might have been a minute and might have been ten, and that, I think, is the part I have never told anyone, and the part I am telling you now.

We left before the maids came. We took the chocolates. We folded the robes and put them on the chair as if we had been raised correctly. On the way down in the elevator he turned the wrong key over in his palm like a coin he was about to flip, and then he slipped it into the brass slot at the front desk while no one was looking, and we walked out into the morning and did not speak about the room again, not that day, not the day after, and not, finally, ever.

He is not in my life now. Neither is the version of me who could have done that. But the room, somehow, still is. I find myself in it on certain evenings, between things — the slow red carpet, the lamp the color of a held breath, the small dark chocolates on the unwanted pillows, the wrong key warm in his hand. I do not want to go back. I want to have been there. There is a difference.
pieces.notes: Hotel-room single-night memory, told from years later; the wrong-key conceit makes the night feel borrowed/permitted; refuses to describe the sex itself, only the framing.

pieces.title: Closing Time at the Astoria
pieces.excerpt: I had not seen her in nine years when she walked into the empty theatre with the keys in her hand and the same way of holding her cigarette between the second and third fingers, as if the cigarette were something she had agreed to keep for someone else.
pieces.body:
I had not seen her in nine years when she walked into the empty theatre with the keys in her hand and the same way of holding her cigarette between the second and third fingers, as if the cigarette were something she had agreed to keep for someone else.

The Astoria was closing. That was the only reason I had come. They were tearing the building down in March to make a row of glass apartments no one I knew would ever live in, and the old projectionist, who had been my friend in the years when I had a great many friends, had written to a small list of us and said, come for the last night, come walk around, the booth is open, the seats are still the velvet ones. I had taken the train down on a Thursday in a coat that was too thin for the weather and a flask of something I did not need and a vague intention to behave myself. The intention had not survived the platform.

She was the manager. I had not known. The projectionist, the old liar, had not told me. He had simply given me the key code for the side door and a time and said, the lobby will be lit, come up the stairs, and I had come up the stairs and there she was at the box-office window, counting something into an envelope, in a black sweater I almost recognized, and when she lifted her head I watched the nine years go through her face in the order they had happened and then collect, quietly, behind her eyes, and stay there.

She said my name. Just the one syllable, the short one, the one only three people on earth had ever used. I said hers. The lobby was the temperature of an old church. The carpet under our feet had been red once and was now the color of a bruise that has been on a body for a week, and the brass of the railings had gone soft and warm with a century of palms.

We did not, at first, touch. I want to be honest about the choreography of the next hour because the choreography was the entire thing. We did not touch in the lobby. We did not touch on the stairs up to the balcony, although we climbed them together and she went first and I watched, against my will and entirely on purpose, the shape of her shoulders move under the black sweater in a way I had not let myself remember in nine years and now remembered all at once, with the shocking clarity of a thing returned intact from a long flood. We did not touch in the balcony either. She showed me her favorite seat, third row from the front, on the aisle, the one with the worn arm where generations of hands had rested through generations of films, and she sat down in it and patted the seat next to her, and I sat down, and our knees, when I crossed my leg, brushed once and did not brush again.

The screen was empty. The house lights were low. Somewhere in the building the projectionist was, I assumed, pretending to be busy. She had brought up a bottle of something amber and two of the small glasses they used to serve at the lobby bar in the years when the Astoria still had a lobby bar, and she poured for both of us with the careful flat wrist of a person who has poured drinks for a living, and we drank the first one fast and the second one slowly and the third one we did not finish.

She asked me what I was doing now. I told her. She told me what she was doing. We had both, in our ways, become quieter people. She had been married, briefly, to a man I had never met and would not, from her telling, have liked. I had moved twice and started a small press that lost money in a dignified way. The facts of nine years took perhaps twenty minutes to exchange, which is the correct ratio, and then there was nothing else to say, and we sat in the velvet dark of the empty balcony and looked at the blank screen as if it might, in its own time, begin.

I had forgotten, or had made myself forget, the specific quality of her silences. She had a way of being quiet that was not absence. It was a kind of forward leaning. It made the air between her and whatever she was looking at feel slightly tilted, as if everything were sliding gently in her direction. I had loved her, twelve years before, in a small apartment with bad windows, badly and well, in the way of people who do not yet know that loving someone is a skill and not a weather. We had ended, the first time, over something so trivial I cannot now reconstruct it, and then properly, later, over the larger things the trivial thing had been standing in for. I had not, in nine years, allowed myself the sentence: I would still.

She turned her head. She did not turn her body, only her head, the way she used to do at parties when she wanted me to leave with her without anyone else knowing, and the small bright animal that had been sleeping in my chest for nine years opened both eyes at once.

She said, do you remember the booth.

I said, I remember the booth.

The booth had been the projectionist's, in the years he had loved us both in the harmless way certain older men love certain younger women, and he had let us, twice, sit in it during late films and watch the reels go around and feel like the secret operators of the entire visible world. It was up a narrow iron staircase behind a door marked STAFF that had been painted over so many times the letters were almost a relief. She stood up. She did not offer me her hand. She simply walked, and I followed, and we went down the balcony stairs and across the back of the house and through the door and up the iron stairs in the dark, and the whole climb she did not look back, and I understood that the not-looking-back was itself the invitation, was the entire grammar of what she was offering, and I followed it the way one follows a sentence one has been waiting for years to hear completed.

The booth was warm. The old projector sat in the middle of it like a sleeping animal, its great round eyes empty, and there was a small window onto the dark house, and a stool, and a shelf of film cans no one would ever load again. She closed the door behind us. She did not lock it. There was no one to lock it against. She turned to face me in the small warm dark and she put one hand, finally, against the side of my neck, just below the jaw, where the pulse lives, and she held it there, and she did not move.

I will not tell you what we did. I will tell you that the projector smelled of oil and old heat. I will tell you that at one point I laughed, soundlessly, into her hair, because I could not believe the simple ridiculous luck of being thirty-eight and being touched, in the dark, by the one person whose touch I had spent nine years pretending I had grown out of needing. I will tell you that she said something against my mouth that I have never repeated to another human being and will not repeat now, and that the saying of it was, more than anything else that happened in that room, the thing that undid me.

We came down the iron stairs in the small grey hour before opening, which the Astoria would not have. The projectionist was asleep in the back row of the orchestra with his coat over him like a child. We did not wake him. She walked me to the side door. She did not kiss me again. She put her forehead, just for a second, against my forehead, and we stood like that, breathing the same small column of air, and then she opened the door and I went out into the wet street and the door closed behind me with the soft definitive sound of an old building that knows how to close.

In March they tore it down. I did not go to watch. She wrote to me, once, in the spring, a single line on a postcard with no return address: I am glad you came. I have the postcard in a drawer. I have not written back. I do not know if I will. I know that the not-writing is, at this point, its own kind of letter, and that she, of all people, will know how to read it.
pieces.notes: Reunion short story in a closing theatre; queer F/F narrator; the choreography of not-touching builds the tension, with the projection booth as the held-breath climax; reunion left ambiguous.

pieces.title: Inventory of a Long Mistake
pieces.excerpt: We agreed, in the beginning, that there would be no calendar. Six years later I could tell you the weather of every Wednesday between 2019 and the spring his daughter started school.
pieces.body:
We agreed, in the beginning, that there would be no calendar. Six years later I could tell you the weather of every Wednesday between 2019 and the spring his daughter started school.

*

The first time it was a coat-check. A friend's wedding, a basement room, a number on a small brass disk. He took my coat from the woman at the counter and held it for me as if I were leaving, although I had only just come down the stairs to escape the speeches, and the gesture stopped time so cleanly that we both noticed, and noticing was the entire beginning.

*

He was married. I want to say that first because I will not be saying it again. He was married, and I knew, and she knew nothing, and I have, in the years since, tried on every version of myself that this fact requires and found that none of them quite fit and I wear them anyway.

*

We met in restaurants in the wrong neighborhood. We met in the back rooms of bookstores. We met, twice, in the lobby of a hotel where neither of us was a guest, and sat in the leather chairs by the fireplace and did not touch and ordered tea we did not drink, and the not-touching, in those public rooms with the heavy carpets and the careful waitstaff, was a thing we did to each other on purpose, the way another couple might have lit candles.

*

The first afternoon I let him into my apartment he stood for a full minute in the doorway with his coat still on and looked, not at me, but at the room behind me — the small kitchen, the window, the chair I read in — as if he were memorizing an address he was forbidden to write down. Then he took the coat off himself. He did not let me take it. I understood, later, that this was a courtesy: he was not going to ask me to be the wife of his hours with me. He was going to remove his own coat. He was going to hang it on my hook with his own hands. He was going to be, in my one room, a man without a household for as long as the afternoon would let him.

*

What we did, what we did not do — I am not going to give you the catalogue. I will say that he was a slow man. I will say that his slowness was not a technique. It was a kind of attention, the same attention he brought to the menu in restaurants and to the spines of books on my shelf, a willingness to be in the room with a thing for as long as the thing required. I have never, before or since, been looked at the way he looked at me in the half hour before he touched me. It ruined, I think, several subsequent kindnesses from better men.

*

Wednesdays. Always Wednesdays, for the first year. He had a standing meeting that ran from one to three and a child to collect at five, and the two hours between were the country we built together, the small republic with the kitchen and the window and the chair. We learned each other on Wednesdays. We learned each other's coffee, each other's silences, each other's particular way of laughing at the wrong part of a sentence. By the fourth month I could tell from the sound of his step in the stairwell what kind of week he had been having. By the sixth, he could tell from the angle of my shoulders whether I had been crying that morning, and would not ask, and would simply put the kettle on, and that was its own kind of being known.

*

There was a Wednesday in February when the heat in my building broke. He came up in his good coat and we sat on the floor under three blankets with our hands wrapped around the same cup and he told me, into the steam, about a thing his father had done to him when he was nine that I do not have permission to repeat, and I told him, into the same steam, the corresponding thing of mine, and we did not touch each other for the whole two hours, and walked away from that afternoon more naked than from any of the others.

*

I did not, ever, ask him to leave her. I want this entered into the record. Not because I was noble. I was not noble. I did not ask because I knew, with the clean instinct one only has about the loves that are damaging one in real time, that the entire structure of what we had was being held up by the wall of the marriage, and that if you pulled the wall away the structure would simply lie down. We were a thing that could only exist in a corridor. I knew it. He knew it. We never said so. The not-saying was, by year three, a discipline we practiced as carefully as anything else.

*

There were two times I almost ended it. The first was after a dinner I had eaten alone, badly, at a counter, on a Tuesday in October, and had walked home through a rain that felt personal, and had sat on my own bed in my coat and said out loud to the empty apartment, this is not a life, this is the shape of a life. I wrote him a message that night I did not send. I read it now sometimes. It is the best thing I have ever written and I will never publish it.

*

The second time was the morning his daughter started school. He told me, in the chair by the window, with the particular flat voice he used for the facts of his other life, and I felt something in my chest go very quiet, the way a room goes quiet when an appliance one had not noticed was running shuts off. I had not known he was going to tell me. I had not known I was going to mind. I minded. I stood up and made more coffee neither of us wanted and I stood at the counter with my back to him and I did not cry, and he did not come to me, because he understood, correctly, that being come to in that moment would have ended us, and we stayed in the room together in our two separate silences for what might have been five minutes, and then I turned around, and he held out his hand from the chair, and I went.

*

The geographies. His left wrist had a small white scar shaped like a comma. There was a particular hollow at the base of my throat he was, I think, in love with on its own terms, as if it were a small independent person he had been introduced to and had liked. He could not whistle. I could not, in his presence, lie. Neither of us learned the other's middle name until year four, and when we finally exchanged them, in bed, in a low light, it felt obscene in a way that nothing else we did ever quite managed.

*

The end was not dramatic. I want you to understand. The end was a Wednesday like the others, in the fifth October, and he came up the stairs at the usual time, and we sat in the usual chairs, and somewhere in the middle of an unimportant sentence about a book neither of us had finished I understood, and he understood that I understood, and we did not, even then, say it. He stayed the full two hours. He drank the coffee. He put the cup in the sink himself. He took his coat off the hook with his own hands and he put it on with his own hands, and at the door he turned and he looked at me for a long moment in the grey light from the window, and he said, thank you, which was a sentence he had never said to me in five years, and which I understood, then and now, to mean everything.

*

He did not write. I did not write. We have not, in two years, been in a room together. I saw him once, across a street, in a coat I did not recognize, walking with the daughter who must now be reading on her own. He did not see me. I stood very still on my side of the street until he had turned the corner, and then I went into the shop I had been going into and I bought the thing I had been going to buy, and I walked home, and I made the dinner, and I ate it at the counter, and the apartment did not feel empty, exactly, but it felt — accurately, finally, for the first time in six years — like mine.

*

I am not sorry. I want this entered into the record too. I am not sorry, and I am not proud, and I do not, on most days, think about him. On the days I do, I think about the coat. I think about the hook by the door. I think about the slow precise way he put his own coat on his own body when the afternoons were over, and how that gesture, which I once read as discretion, I now understand to have been a kind of grief he was practicing in advance, every Wednesday, for five years, so that when the last Wednesday came he would know how to leave.
pieces.notes: Anonymous narrator, six-year affair told in numbered/asterisked fragments; the coat as recurring image carrying the moral weight; refuses both melodrama and absolution.
